events.text: I want to grow a backyard vegetable garden
Finding the first contact a pro would call…

Hi, I'm Sarah, a Master Gardener who helps folks start backyard vegetable gardens. 'Veggie garden' can mean a few raised beds, a full in-ground plot, or even containers on a patio. What's your situation looking like?
Raised beds in the yard
I want to grow a backyard vegetable garden (raised beds in the yard)
Got it. For that I'm bringing in 5 Pros. Sun and soil dictate what's possible, so Diana and Marcus go first; then Priya picks crops, Jamal waters them, Rachel protects them.
Hi, I'm Diana, your site & sun analyst. Maps sunlight, microclimate, and site constraints.
Hi, I'm Marcus, your soil & compost specialist. Owns soil health, amendments, and drainage.
Hi, I'm Priya, your vegetable varietal curator. Picks crops matched to goals, climate, and skill.
Hi, I'm Jamal, your irrigation designer. Plans watering systems and water conservation.
Hi, I'm Rachel, your integrated pest manager. Handles pest, disease, and wildlife defense.
How many hours of direct sun does your spot get?
8+ hours
How much growing space are you working with?
100 to 400 sq ft
What do you know about your current soil quality?
Totally unknown
Do you have access to compost or organic matter?
Need to start
Diana noted you have 8+ hours of sun. Which vegetables matter most to you?
Tomatoes & peppers, Herbs
How much gardening experience do you have?
Killed a few plants
Priya's planning around your tomatoes & peppers, herbs picks. How do you want to handle watering?
Soaker hoses
Which critters visit your yard?
Squirrels, Just bugs
That's everything we need up front. Give us a moment while your Staff writes up your plan.
Your Staff is writing your plan…
Your plan is ready.

sun: With 8+ hours sun, you can grow nearly any warm-season crop including tomatoes and peppers.
At 100 to 400 sq ft, plan 2 to 4 raised beds, each 4 ft wide max so you can reach the middle.
Watch afternoon shade from fences or neighbor's house in July; map shadows across one full day before building.
soil: Since soil is unknown, send a sample to your county extension office for a $15 to $25 test before planting.
Fill raised beds with a 60/30/10 mix of topsoil, compost, and aeration like perlite, roughly 10 to 12 inches deep.
Start a compost pile now with browns and greens at a 3:1 ratio; finished compost takes 3 to 6 months.
veg: For a beginner, stick to 2 or 3 determinate tomatoes like Celebrity or Roma and sweet peppers; skip hot peppers unless you love them.
Add basil, parsley, chives, and oregano; basil near tomatoes helps both flavor and pest control.
Buy transplants your first year instead of starting from seed; it cuts failure risk by half.
water: Soaker hoses are perfect since they keep foliage dry and prevent fungal issues like blight on tomatoes.
Run hoses 30 to 45 minutes, 2 to 3 times weekly; aim for 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week total.
Mulch beds with 2 to 3 inches of straw or shredded leaves to cut watering needs by 30 to 50 percent.
pest: Squirrels dig for the smell of fresh soil; cover beds with chicken wire or hardware cloth for the first 2 weeks after planting.
For bugs, scout weekly and hand-pick hornworms and aphids; reach for neem or insecticidal soap only if damage spreads.
Install a simple 2 ft chicken wire fence if rabbits appear; depends on your neighborhood pressure.

steps: Sarah maps the sunniest 100 to 400 sq ft zone and sketches 2 or 3 raised bed locations by mid-November.
Diana walks the yard at 10am, 1pm, and 4pm on a clear day to confirm 8+ hours of direct sun.
Marcus mails a soil test to the county extension and starts a compost pile before winter sets in.
Sarah builds or orders 4x8 ft raised bed kits and fills them with the 60/30/10 mix by late March.
Priya buys 3 tomato and 2 pepper transplants plus herb starts after the last frost in May.
Jamal lays soaker hoses on a timer and tops beds with 2 to 3 inches of straw mulch at planting.
